sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large foundation models have accelerated progress toward general-purpose agents that interact with humans and other agents through language and multimodal signals. However, robust multi-agent decision-making requires reasoning about what other agents know, intend, and are likely to do under partial observability. Current agentic systems often operate through prompt design, memory, or end-to-end behavioral shaping, but typically do not learn an explicit partner-state representation that can be reused as a decision variable across tasks. We introduce \emph{mental-model-enabled agents}, a framework that equips an agent with a latent mental model of its counterpart, allowing it to infer hidden beliefs, intentions, and likely reactions from the observed history and use these inferences to guide action selection. Our method learns an amortized recursive Theory-of-Mind representation, with first- and second-order mental-state structure, jointly with a belief-conditioned reward model that evaluates candidate actions relative to the inferred partner state. A policy is then learned under this belief-aware signal, yielding an agent that can act independently at inference time while retaining the benefits of explicit partner modeling. We evaluate the same framework on both language-only and multimodal benchmarks. Across these settings, explicit mental-state modeling consistently improves interaction quality and Theory-of-Mind performance over base agentic systems, showing that structured partner modeling is a useful inductive bias for general multi-agent systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hananshafi/Mental-Models

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern AI, robotics, and cognitive science increasingly converge on shared objective: building agents that can reason, plan, and act effectively in the world. The core idea is that intelligent systems, both biological and artificial, must construct mental models of the world. This is in line with Kenneth Craiks seminal work The Nature of Explanation, which proposed that organisms maintain small-scale internal representations of external reality [3]. Such mental models allow them to simulate possible actions, anticipate outcomes, and adapt effectively to changing environments. However, in interactive environments, the world is partly constituted by other agents whose goals, beliefs, and strategies are not directly observable. As result, successful action requires modeling not only the environment, but also other minds, capacity commonly studied as Theory of Mind (ToM) [8]. In humans, ToM is mediated by compact representations of partners latent mental states that support prediction and planning [8]. This perspective has motivated computational approaches that learn agent models directly from behavioral traces. ToMnet [22], for instance, showed that an observer can infer latent agent properties from past trajectories and use them to predict future behavior, demonstrating the value of explicit uncertainty over unobserved mental state and amortized inference that adapts rapidly to novel agents. These properties are particularly valuable in multi-agent settings, where partial observability is fundamental. Large foundation models have accelerated progress toward general-purpose agents that interact with humans and other agents through language and multimodal signals. Yet robust interactive competence remains difficult. An agent must infer what other agents know, want, and are likely to do, and choose actions that improve outcomes under partial observability  (Fig.1)  . Depending on the setting, this may involve cooperation, negotiation, assistance, competition, or adherence to conventions and norms. Empirically, despite strong conversational ability, current LLMs lag behind humans on core ingredients of interactive reasoning, including Theory-of-Mind-style inference [23, 29, 26], adherence to interaction norms [31], and robust performance across goal-driven multi-agent scenarios [36]. Humans succeed in such settings because they rapidly form and update beliefs about others from limited evidence [13, 28]. By contrast, current LLM agents typically do not maintain an explicit model of partners hidden goals, beliefs, or strategies. As result, they may misread intent, commit to brittle plans, and struggle to adapt when the interaction unfolds in unexpected ways. Most prior work on LLM-based multi-agent systems improves behavior through shaping or scaffolding rather than explicit partner-state estimation. Existing approaches include instruction tuning and preference-based reinforcement learning that steer generation [19, 25, 30], prompt-level mechanisms such as self-critique, reflection, and memory that condition the agent on textual summaries of prior interaction [1, 20], and multi-turn synthetic self-play that induces complex interaction skills such as consensus-building [18]. Across these approaches, partner dynamics are represented only implicitly either in the prompt text or trajectory summaries and not embedded in policys latent dynamics. The result is the absence of an explicit belief state with clear semantics and quantified uncertainty, which limits interpretability, complicates reuse across tasks, and prevents partner modeling from being integrated systematically into different policy learners. long line of work in sequential decision-making under partial observability suggests that effective multi-agent behavior depends on maintaining beliefs over hidden state, including other agents objectives, information states, and internal models [12, 5, 6]. Extending this principle to foundationmodel agents is nontrivial. When beliefs about partner are expressed only as short natural-language hypotheses or serialized summaries appended to prompts, they remain limited in expressivity, and downstream action selection becomes tightly coupled to prompt formulation. This motivates the central question of our work: can an agent learn an amortized latent belief state from interaction history and use it as stable training signal for multi-agent policy learning? In this paper, we address this question with mental-model-enabled agents for multi-agent systems under partial observability. Our approach learns compact latent belief state from interaction history that captures hidden variables of other agents, including goals, beliefs, knowledge, strategies, and higher-order expectations. We then learn reward model that evaluates candidate actions relative to this inferred state, rather than only the observable context. The resulting belief-conditioned reward is 2 used to train policy under the learned mental model, while the final policy remains standalone at inference time. Together, these components define general framework for ToM-guided decision making in multi-agent systems across diverse settings. To validate the generality of our method, we evaluate it on both language-only and multimodal benchmarks for multi-agent systems. For language-only settings, we consider SOTOPIA [36], CRAIGSLIST-BARGAIN [9], TOMI [15], and BIGTOM [7]; for multimodal evaluation, we use MMROLE [4]. We also convert existing resources into ToM-supervised training data by augmenting them with mental-state annotations; Appendix Table 10 summarizes the additional supervision relative to the original releases. Across these benchmarks, explicit mental-state modeling consistently improves downstream performance. For example, on SOTOPIA, our approach with Qwen2.5-7B achieves an average relative gain of 11.5% over the base model across two partner settings, while on BIGTOM it improves paired TB/FB accuracy by 26.7 pp on average across the six reported settings. In summary, our contributions are: We propose general framework for ToM-guided multi-agent systems under partial observability, in which an agent learns an explicit latent belief state over other agents from observed history and uses it to support downstream decision making. We introduce recursive mental-state architecture and coupled mental-state/reward learning objective that make firstand second-order partner representations directly useful for evaluating candidate actions. We show how the learned mental signal can be distilled into standalone policies, so that explicit partner modeling improves training while deployment remains efficient. We evaluate the framework across language-only and multimodal benchmarks, and augment these resources with additional ToM supervision, utility signals, rationales, and hard negatives to support training and analysis.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multi-agent systems. Recent work has explored LLM-based multi-agent systems in which multiple agents coordinate through role specialization, dialogue, memory, and tool use. CAMEL studies cooperative role-conditioned interactions in an agent society setting [16]. MetaGPT, ChatDev, and AutoGen emphasize structured workflows, standardized operating procedures, and programmable conversation patterns for collaborative problem solving [10, 21, 32]. These systems improve performance mainly through external orchestration, such as role decomposition, protocol design, and tool integration. Our work is complementary: rather than modifying only the interaction protocol, we focus on internal partner modeling under partial observability by learning latent belief state and using it to shape downstream control. Interactive environments and agent training. Another line of work develops environments and training pipelines for interactive agents. SOTOPIA [36] provides open-ended, multi-turn interactions with private goals and multidimensional evaluation, and subsequent work studies imitation and self-reinforcement, utterance-level reward design, and scalable simulation in this setting [36, 30, 34, 35]. In the multimodal setting, MMROLE introduces framework for developing and evaluating multimodal role-playing agents using persona-grounded images, dialogues, and reward-model-based evaluation [4]. These works provide important testbeds and training recipes for interactive agents, but they generally do not learn an explicit amortized partner model that is reused as decision variable across benchmarks. Our approach instead learns latent partner representation from interaction history, couples it with reward modeling, and distills the resulting signal into policy. Theory of Mind and agent modeling. ToM aims to infer or represent agents latent mental states (beliefs, goals, intentions) to predict future behavior and mental states. ToMnet [22] learns latent models of agents from behavioral traces to predict future actions and agent-specific characteristics. In language-only settings, ToMi, BigToM, ToMBench, and OpenToM provide increasingly controlled or comprehensive evaluations of belief tracking and mental-state reasoning [15, 7, 2, 33]. SymbolicToM shows that explicit belief tracking can substantially improve ToM reasoning at decoding time [24]. In multimodal settings, MMToM-QA and MuMA-ToM extend ToM evaluation beyond text, and MuMA-ToM further introduces LIMP, model-based inverse multi-agent planning approach for multimodal mental-state inference [11, 27]. Relative to this literature, our contribution is not new 3 Figure 2: Method overview. Phase 1 jointly learns an amortized recursive mental-model and mental-conditioned reward model from multi-agent context. The latent contains firstand secondorder belief, intent, and thought subspaces, which condition reward prediction. Phase 2 freezes the mental-state encoder and reward model, scores sampled policy actions with the learned mental reward, and optimizes the policy with mental-reward guidance. Phase 3 deploys only the trained policy in the multi-agent setting. ToM benchmark or task-specific inference procedure. Instead, we learn an amortized latent mental state from interaction history, couple it to utility prediction, and use the resulting signal to train policies for general multi-agent interaction across both language-only and multimodal benchmarks.

sections.title: 4 Experimentation
sections.content: Implementation details. All trained open-source agents use LoRA adapters on 7B-scale language or vision-language backbones. We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the primary language backbone, including LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 as additional SOTOPIA comparisons, and use Qwen2.5-VL-Chat for multimodal experiments on MMRole. For SOTOPIA, we augment SOTOPIA-π[30] episodes with ToM labels and utility annotations to train the mental-state/reward model; for BigToM and ToMi, we train on 5K synthetic BigToM-style samples and evaluate on the official BIGTOM and TOMI splits; for MMROLE, we augment the released training set with mental labels. CRAIGSLIST-BARGAIN and FANTOM are used only as transfer evaluations. We first train the mental-state/reward model and then optimize the policy with supervised warmup when used, followed by mental-reward-guided GRPO using rewards from the frozen scorer. Detailed data construction, sample counts, latent dimensions, optimizer settings, decoding parameters, and hardware are reported in Appendix A.1.3; Appendix Table 10 summarizes the augmented supervision, and Appendix A.2.4 reports automated filtering and blinded human verification. Baselines and evaluation. For SOTOPIA, we compare against zero-shot/base LLaMA2-7B, Mistral7B, and Qwen2.5-7B agents, SFT and GRPO variants trained on our generated data, and closed-source GPT-4o-mini/Gemini baselines, evaluating with the official episode-level seven-dimension SOTOPIA scoring protocol on all, hard, and partner-averaged settings. Craigslist-Bargain uses the released negotiation protocol and reports deal, walkaway, and no-agreement rates. For BigToM and ToMi, we follow the official evaluation scripts and report the released TB/FB/TBFB, Average, Joint, and false-belief split metrics against GPT-style and classic ToMi baselines where available. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced mental-model-enabled agent framework for multi-agent systems, where an agent learns an amortized recursive Theory-of-Mind latent state and couples it to belief-conditioned reward model. The resulting reward signal is used to train policies that act independently at test time while retaining the benefits of explicit partner-state modeling. Across SOTOPIA, negotiation transfer, BIGTOM/TOMI/FANTOM, and MMROLE, the same framework improves open-source agents on social-interaction and Theory-of-Mind benchmarks. Our results also show that augmenting existing datasets with mental-state annotations, utility signals, rationales, and contrastive negatives provides useful supervision for learning reusable partner representations. Limitations and future work. Our training environments are primarily dyadic; the zero-shot FANTOM transfer in Appendix A.3 provides initial multi-party evidence, while end-to-end multiparty training with participant-specific latent updates remains future work. The same formulation can also be extended beyond language and image-grounded role play to embodied and robotic settings, where partner beliefs, goals, visibility, and physical constraints evolve over longer horizons. Finally, scaling to larger policies, more diverse partner models, richer online belief updates, and human-in-theloop evaluation would help test how far explicit mental-state structure continues to improve robust multi-agent behavior.

MMROLE [4] is multimodal role-playing benchmark consisting of 85 characters, 11K images, and 14K single or multi-turn dialogues, yielding 85K training samples. Characters span fictional figures (Marvel heroes, Harry Potter, Friends), real historical persons (Kobe Bryant, Leonardo da Vinci), and Chinese historical figures. Each episode pairs character profile (including personality, life story, relationships, and catchphrases) with real image from COCO or movie/TV scripts. Three dialogue types are covered: comment (a character comments on an image), humanrole (a human and character discuss an image), and inter-role (two characters interact about an image). The original dataset evaluates role-playing quality across eight dimensions: coherency, fluency, image-text relevance, instruction adherence, knowledge consistency, personality consistency, response accuracy, and tone consistency. Augmentation. We focus exclusively on inter-role dialogues and apply three-step pipeline to add visual theory-of-mind annotations. Step 1 Per-turn restructuring: Each inter-role dialogue is decomposed into per-turn snapshots. Each turn contains the speaker and partner profiles, the image, the full dialogue history up to that turn, and the current utterance, producing 36,744 per-turn examples. First-order beliefs: what the speaker believes the partner is visually attending to and intending. 19 Second-order beliefs: what the speaker believes the partner believes about the speaker. Belief probes: structured question-answer pairs across five types (visual percept, first-order belief, second-order belief, intent inference, false belief) at three difficulty levels. A.4 Impact Statement This work studies explicit mental-model representations for multi-agent systems. The main positive impact is to make agent behavior more interpretable and controllable in settings where an agent must reason about another agents goals, beliefs, knowledge, or visual perspective. Such representations can support safer assistants, better negotiation and collaboration agents, and clearer diagnostic tools for evaluating whether model is relying on task-relevant social and perceptual signals rather than surface imitation. Our augmented datasets also provide structured supervision for studying Theory-of-Mind behavior across language-only and multimodal benchmarks. The same capability also carries risks. Models that infer or exploit another agents latent state could be misused for manipulation, persuasion, privacy invasion, or profiling, especially if deployed in high-stakes human-facing settings. The inferred variables in our framework should therefore be treated as task-conditioned modeling constructs, not as ground-truth psychological states. They may reflect annotation bias, dataset artifacts, or stereotypes in the underlying models and data. For this reason, deployment should include consent-aware data collection, privacy filtering, bias audits, uncertainty reporting, and restrictions against using inferred mental states for sensitive decisions about individuals. Our experiments are limited to benchmark and synthetic/augmented training settings, and future work should study human oversight and safety constraints before using such systems in real-world multi-agent applications.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to section 4 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to section 6 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] 27 Justification: The paper does not include theoretical results Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to sections 4, A.2, and A.1.3 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 28 Answer: [No] Justification: We will release the code, models and data upon acceptance. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to sections 4,A.2 and A.1.3 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper reports official benchmark scores under fixed evaluation protocols and includes paired Wilcoxon significance test for the MMROLE visual-grounding analysis in Appendix 12. For SOTOPIA, we repeated the main evaluations multiple times and observed nearly identical aggregate scores, suggesting low evaluation variance under the fixed protocol. However, we do not report formal run-to-run error bars or confidence intervals for all main trained-policy comparisons, since repeating full 7B-scale LLM/VLM training and closed-source evaluations across multiple seeds is computationally and API-cost intensive. We therefore treat the main benchmark tables as point estimates and support the claims through consistency across benchmarks, model families, held-out splits, repeated SOTOPIA evaluations, and ablations. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. 29 The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to sections 4, A.1.3 and A.2 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes paper conforms with NeurIPS code of ethics Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to section A. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. 30 If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: All the models and data used in the paper are publicly available. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to sections 1, 2 and 4 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. 31 If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Refer to sections 4, A.1.3 and A.2 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve any experiments with humans Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. 32 We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [No] Justification: We did not use LLM for any method specific ideas Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
